title: How to Generate Mergeable Code with a Context Engine — Peter Werry, Unblocked

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk centers on Unblocked's context engine, which constructs, curates, and supplies organizational context to coding agents like Claude Code, with explicit discussion of context limits, satisfaction of search, and per-task context building. Applied to software engineering workflows: Claude Code, GitHub PR history, code review agents, and engineering social graphs. Shown operating against a live production codebase and running as a cloud agent that produced a real fix PR, not a research prototype. Assumes comfort with agent coding tools, MCP/skills, and code review workflows, but explains the underlying context-engine concept for new listeners. Conference talk built almost entirely around live demos with a single speaker narrating. Includes quantitative comparisons (~$1/1min with engine vs ~2x time/cost without; 50% fewer tokens customer quote) drawn from observed demo runs rather than published benchmarks.

summary:
Peter Werry positions Unblocked as building a 'context engine' that delivers organizational context to humans and increasingly to agents. He frames the pre-agent era as one where engineers were the context layer: trolling discussions, reading code, accumulating tribal knowledge, and surviving incidents. Agents invert this by behaving like expert new employees who reset every task and must rediscover how the organization builds, tests, and deploys. Werry sketches an AI maturity curve from autocomplete, through IDE tools and organizational wikis, to MCP-and-skills usage, and ultimately software factories requiring continuous delivery of context to handle unknown unknowns.

He borrows the radiology term 'satisfaction of search' to argue that agents attached to wikis will find a plausible artifact and stop. They also fail to distill understanding of how dependencies interact or how architectural plans scope future work. Stuffing entire codebases and docs into a million-token window doesn't help: context exceeds capacity and distracts the agent. The visible iceberg tip is code; the submerged mass includes intent, team conventions, past decisions, Slack discussions, and architecture rationale.

In a live demo, Werry asks about an internal 'source mark engine' component. The system articulates the architecture, generates a diagram that did not previously exist, and surfaces sources so humans can verify the answer. He shows Slack integration where the engine listens and responds, and pivots to agents in Claude Code. Asking for an optimization plan on the source mark calculator, he contrasts runs without and with the engine: with it, the plan costs under a dollar and runs in roughly a minute, pulling PR, Slack, Notion, and architecture context; without it, the run takes about double the time and more cost because the agent must discover more and often discovers the wrong things, causing compounding loops later in execution.

He then introduces a review agent that uses reviewer seniority as a signal to boost important comments. When a drop in flagged issues occurred after switching to a different model, Unblocked ran as a cloud agent with full organizational context, generated a fix PR, and correlated the drop directly to a Slack conversation from a senior engineer (Richie), tracing from surfaced issues back through history to a final PR.

Werry closes by highlighting two open-source projects: a document query engine that ingests GitHub pull request history, synthesizes a schema from sampled documents, and answers queries via agent chat; and an engineering social graph that clusters review relationships across the codebase, surfaces coverage holes, and feeds into the context engine itself. He also mentions a context engine simulator for per-task context experiments and a colleague's follow-up talk, landing on a customer quote: 50% fewer tokens, faster triage, better answers.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: Unblocked builds a 'context engine' that supplies organizational context to humans and agents, not just data access.
Pre-agent, engineers were the context layer; agents behave like expert new hires who reset knowledge per task.
AI maturity runs from autocomplete, to IDE tools, to wikis, to MCP/skills, to software factories needing continuous context.
Agents suffer 'satisfaction of search': they find a plausible answer in a wiki and stop, missing other indicators.
Million-token windows don't solve context: the corpus is too large and distracts the agent from task-specific flow.
Same Claude Code optimization plan: ~$1 and ~1 min with the context engine vs ~2x time and higher cost without it; bad early discoveries compound later.
A cloud Unblocked agent traced a post-switch drop in flagged issues to a senior engineer's Slack conversation and produced a fix PR.
Open-source offerings include a GitHub PR document query engine, an engineering social graph, and a context engine simulator.

Describe how satisfaction of search manifests in agentic code retrieval

sections.title: Setting up the context engine and the pre-agent era
sections.summary: Werry introduces Unblocked's context engine, frames the pre-agent era where engineers were the context layer, and explains that agents behave like new employees who reset every task.

sections.title: AI maturity curve and the move toward software factories
sections.summary: He outlines a maturity curve from autocomplete through wikis and MCP/skills to software factories, arguing that context, not access, is the bottleneck as automation scales.

sections.title: Satisfaction of search and the iceberg of intent
sections.summary: He borrows the radiology term 'satisfaction of search' to explain why agents stop at plausible wiki answers, notes they don't distill understanding, and argues million-token windows distract rather than help. He sketches the iceberg of code versus intent, conventions, decisions, Slack, and architecture rationale.

sections.title: Live demo: human question answering with generated diagrams
sections.summary: Werry demos asking about the internal 'source mark engine', showing a generated architecture diagram that didn't previously exist, with sources attached for verification. He also shows a Slack integration where the engine can chime in or be addressed directly.

sections.title: Agents in Claude Code: same plan with and without context engine
sections.summary: He pivots to agents, generating an optimization plan for the source mark calculator in Claude Code twice. With Unblocked, the plan costs under a dollar and runs in about a minute; without it, the run takes roughly double the time and costs more because the agent discovers more and often the wrong things, causing compounding loops later.

sections.title: Review agent and debugging surfaced issues (intro)
sections.summary: He introduces a code review agent that uses reviewer seniority as a signal to boost important comments, citing an example where it surfaced a senior engineer's prior comment, and begins a story about debugging a drop in surfaced review issues.

sections.title: Cloud agent traces an issues drop to a Slack conversation
sections.summary: Werry demos Unblocked running as a cloud agent with full organizational context. It diagnoses a drop in flagged issues after switching to a different Claude model, correlates the drop directly to a Slack conversation from a senior engineer (Richie), and produces a fix PR tied to the conversation history.

sections.title: Open source: document query engine and engineering social graph
sections.summary: He highlights two open-source projects: a document query engine that ingests GitHub pull request history, synthesizes a schema from sampled documents, and answers queries via agent chat; and an engineering social graph that clusters review relationships, surfaces coverage holes, and feeds into the context engine itself.

sections.title: Context engine simulator and closing
sections.summary: Werry promotes a context engine simulator for per-task with/without context experiments, points to a colleague's follow-up talk, and lands on a customer quote: 50% fewer tokens, faster triage, better answers.

organization.name: Unblocked
organization.summary: Unblocked is an independent Vancouver-based company that builds a context engine for software engineering teams. First-party pages describe a platform that connects source code, docs, tickets, conversations, and production signals, then injects synthesized, permission-aware context into coding agents and developer Q&A. The homepage markets Unblocked as the context layer for modern engineering teams; docs state it is a context engine rather than a search index, delivered via MCP, CLI, Slack, web, and API. Peter Werry is a founding engineer there and demos the owned Context Engine, cloud agent, review agent, and related open-source tools. Claude Code and other coding agents are mentioned clients, not the implementation owner.
organization.status: Independent company as of the research date. getunblocked.com, docs.getunblocked.com, and the Context Engine product page are live. LinkedIn company page lists founding in 2021 and 11-50 employees. No ownership change since the August 2026 talk.
